from kubex.client import create_client
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.container import Container
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.pod import Pod
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.pod_spec import PodSpec
from kubex_core.models.metadata import ObjectMetadata

NAMESPACE = "default"


async def main() -> None:
    client = await create_client()
    async with client:
        api: Api[Pod] = Api(Pod, client=client, namespace=NAMESPACE)
        pod = await api.create(
            Pod(
                metadata=ObjectMetadata(generate_name="example-pod-"),
                spec=PodSpec(containers=[Container(name="example", image="nginx")]),
            ),
        )
        assert pod.metadata.name is not None

        try:
            print(pod)
            print(await api.metadata.get(pod.metadata.name))
            print(await api.metadata.list())
        finally:
            await api.delete(pod.metadata.name)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import asyncio

    asyncio.run(main())

Note

All Kubernetes resources are fully typed Pydantic models. pod.spec, pod.status, and pod.metadata all have proper type annotations — no dict[str, Any] anywhere.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Concepts: Api[T] — generics, namespace/cluster scope, the Ellipsis sentinel
  • Concepts: Configuration — kubeconfig file parsing, in-cluster auth, exec provider
  • Operations: CRUD — get, list, create, replace, delete, delete_collection
  • Operations: Watch — streaming resource events

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
This section covers the full set of operations you can perform on Kubernetes resources with Kubex. Read the Concepts section first if you are new to the library.

  • CRUD

    get, list, create, replace, delete, and delete_collection — the core Kubernetes resource lifecycle operations with filtering, pagination, and deletion options.

  • Watch

    Long-lived watch() streams, WatchEvent and EventType, bookmark events, the sendInitialEvents pattern, and the restart-on-410-Gone recipe.

  • Patch

    All three patch strategies: MergePatch, StrategicMergePatch, and JsonPatch (RFC 6902) with its fluent builder API and JSON Pointer paths.

  • Timeouts

    Timeout, TimeoutTypes, client-level vs per-call configuration, the Ellipsis sentinel, and guidance for long-lived watch streams.

docs.title: CRUD Operations
docs.text: Api[ResourceType] exposes the full set of Kubernetes CRUD operations as async methods. Every method returns the server-side resource (or a Status for deletions), fully parsed by Pydantic.

docs.title: get
docs.text:
Fetch a single resource by name:

from kubex.api import Api
from kubex.client import create_client
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.pod import Pod

client = await create_client()
async with client:
    api: Api[Pod] = Api(Pod, client=client, namespace="default")
    pod = await api.get("my-pod")
    print(pod.metadata.name)

Pass resource_version= to pin the read to a specific version; omit it for the current state.

docs.title: Names and namespaces
docs.text:
Every method that targets a single object (get, replace, patch, delete, and every subresource call) requires a non-empty name: passing None or "" raises ValueError("resource name may not be empty") before any request is sent, so delete() can never turn into a collection delete. Names and namespaces are validated like client-go does — ".", ".." and anything containing / or % raise ValueError — and are percent-encoded, so a name such as weird#name addresses exactly that object. An empty namespace (namespace="") is also rejected; use namespace=None for "all namespaces" on list, watch and delete_collection.

local = Pod(
    metadata=ObjectMetadata(generate_name="example-pod-"),
    spec=PodSpec(containers=[Container(name="example", image="nginx")]),
)
created = await api.create(local)
await api.delete(local.metadata.name)  # ValueError: only the server knows the name
await api.delete(created.metadata.name)  # OK: the server-assigned name

docs.title: list
docs.text:
List all resources in a namespace (or cluster-wide):

pods = await api.list()
for pod in pods.items:
    print(pod.metadata.name)

Filter with label_selector= (e.g. "app=nginx") or field_selector= (e.g. "status.phase=Running"). Use limit= and continue_token= for paginated results:

page = await api.list(label_selector="app=nginx", limit=100)
while page.metadata.continue_:
    page = await api.list(
        label_selector="app=nginx", limit=100, continue_token=page.metadata.continue_
    )

Pass namespace=None to list across all namespaces even when the Api instance has a default namespace set:

all_pods = await api.list(namespace=None)

docs.title: create
docs.text:
Create a new resource. The returned object is the server-assigned representation (including metadata.name when generate_name was used):

from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.container import Container
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.pod_spec import PodSpec
from kubex_core.models.metadata import ObjectMetadata

pod = await api.create(
    Pod(
        metadata=ObjectMetadata(generate_name="example-pod-"),
        spec=PodSpec(containers=[Container(name="example", image="nginx")]),
    ),
)
print(pod.metadata.name)  # server-assigned name, e.g. "example-pod-7g4k2"

Pass dry_run=True to validate the request without persisting anything. Pass field_manager= to set the field manager for server-side apply.

docs.title: replace
docs.text:
Replace a resource in its entirety (the get → modify → replace pattern):

current = await api.get("example-pod")
current.metadata.labels = {**(current.metadata.labels or {}), "env": "staging"}
updated = await api.replace("example-pod", current)
print(updated.metadata.labels)

The full object (including resourceVersion) must be present in the payload — the API server uses resourceVersion as an optimistic-concurrency check. If anything else modified the object between the get and the replace (a controller, the kubelet updating a new pod), the server answers 409 Conflict; re-read and retry:

from kubex.core.exceptions import Conflict

for _ in range(5):
    current = await api.get("example-pod")
    current.metadata.labels = {**(current.metadata.labels or {}), "env": "staging"}
    try:
        updated = await api.replace("example-pod", current)
    except Conflict:
        continue
    break

For changes to a few fields, a patch avoids the read-modify-write cycle altogether.

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
Delete a resource by name. The return type is Status | ResourceType: if the resource has finalizers the API server returns the updated object (with deletionTimestamp set) rather than a Status:

result = await api.delete("example-pod")

Control deletion behaviour with optional parameters:

Parameter Description grace_period_seconds Override the resource's terminationGracePeriodSeconds propagation_policy "Foreground", "Background", or "Orphan" preconditions Precondition(uid=..., resource_version=...) for safe deletes dry_run Validate without actually deleting (True or "All") 
from kubex.core.params import Precondition

await api.delete(
    "example-pod",
    grace_period_seconds=0,
    propagation_policy="Foreground",
    preconditions=Precondition(uid=pod.metadata.uid),
)

docs.title: delete_collection
docs.text:
Delete multiple resources matching a selector in a single call:

result = await api.delete_collection(label_selector="app=example-batch")

delete_collection accepts the same filter parameters as list (label_selector, field_selector, limit, continue_token) plus the same deletion options as delete (grace_period_seconds, propagation_policy, preconditions, dry_run).

The return type is Status | ListEntity[ResourceType] — some versions of the Kubernetes API return the deleted list rather than a Status.

Full example from examples/delete_collection.py:

import uuid
from kubex.api import Api
from kubex.client import create_client
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.container import Container
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.pod import Pod
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.pod_spec import PodSpec
from kubex_core.models.metadata import ObjectMetadata


async def main() -> None:
    client = await create_client()
    async with client:
        api: Api[Pod] = Api(Pod, client=client, namespace="default")
        run_id = uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
        label_selector = f"app=example-batch-{run_id}"

        for i in range(3):
            await api.create(
                Pod(
                    metadata=ObjectMetadata(
                        generate_name=f"example-delete-collection-{i}-",
                        labels={"app": f"example-batch-{run_id}"},
                    ),
                    spec=PodSpec(
                        containers=[Container(name="nginx", image="nginx:latest")]
                    ),
                ),
            )

        result = await api.delete_collection(label_selector=label_selector)
        print(f"delete_collection result: {type(result).__name__}")

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
All non-2xx responses raise a subclass of KubexApiError. The most common errors for CRUD operations:

Exception HTTP status Typical cause NotFound 404 Resource does not exist Conflict 409 create on an existing resource, or replace with a stale resourceVersion Forbidden 403 RBAC: the service account lacks permission UnprocessableEntity 422 Validation failure (schema mismatch, required field missing)

See Exceptions for the full hierarchy.

docs.title: Patch
docs.text: api.patch(name, patch) applies a partial update to an existing resource. Kubex supports all four patch types accepted by the Kubernetes API.

docs.title: Patch types
docs.text: Type Import Content-Type MergePatch kubex.core.patch application/merge-patch+json StrategicMergePatch kubex.core.patch application/strategic-merge-patch+json JsonPatch kubex.core.patch application/json-patch+json ApplyPatch kubex.core.patch application/apply-patch+yaml (server-side apply)

docs.title: MergePatch
docs.text:
Merge patch (RFC 7396) replaces the specified keys and removes any key set to null. Keys not present in the patch are left unchanged. Wrap any resource model in MergePatch(...) to apply it:

from kubex.core.patch import MergePatch
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.apps.v1.deployment import Deployment
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.apps.v1.deployment_spec import DeploymentSpec
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.meta.v1.label_selector import LabelSelector
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.pod_spec import PodSpec
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.pod_template_spec import PodTemplateSpec
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.container import Container
from kubex_core.models.metadata import ObjectMetadata

merge_patch = MergePatch(
    Deployment(
        metadata=ObjectMetadata(),  # required by the model; a patch body doesn't need it set
        spec=DeploymentSpec(
            replicas=3,
            selector=LabelSelector(match_labels={"app": "example"}),
            template=PodTemplateSpec(
                metadata=ObjectMetadata(labels={"app": "example"}),
                spec=PodSpec(
                    containers=[Container(name="nginx", image="nginx:latest")]
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )
)
patched = await api.patch("example-deploy", merge_patch)
print(patched.spec.replicas)  # 3

docs.title: StrategicMergePatch
docs.text:
Strategic merge patch is a Kubernetes extension that understands list-merging semantics (e.g., merging containers by name rather than replacing the whole array). Use it when you want to add or update a list element without specifying the full list:

from kubex.core.patch import StrategicMergePatch

strategic_patch = StrategicMergePatch(
    Deployment(
        metadata=ObjectMetadata(
            annotations={"example.com/patched": "true"},
        )
    )
)
patched = await api.patch("example-deploy", strategic_patch)
print(patched.metadata.annotations)

Strategic merge patch is not available for custom resources — use MergePatch or JsonPatch there.

docs.title: JsonPatch
docs.text:
JSON Patch (RFC 6902) describes a sequence of operations (add, remove, replace, move, copy, test) using JSON Pointer paths. Build patches incrementally using the fluent API:

from kubex.core.patch import JsonPatch

json_patch = JsonPatch().add("/metadata/labels/version", "v1")
patched = await api.patch("example-deploy", json_patch)
print(patched.metadata.labels)

All six RFC 6902 operations are supported:

patch = (
    JsonPatch()
    .add("/metadata/labels/env", "staging")
    .replace("/spec/replicas", 2)
    .remove("/metadata/annotations/example.com~1old-key")
    .test("/metadata/name", "example-deploy")
)

docs.title: Building paths with JsonPointer
docs.text:
JsonPointer is accepted anywhere a path string is, and it handles RFC 6901 escaping for you. Build a pointer by chaining the / operator from a base, or from a tuple of unescaped tokens:

from kubex.core.patch import JsonPatch, JsonPointer

# Chained operator — ideal when a fixed prefix is reused
annotation_path = JsonPointer("/metadata") / "annotations" / "example.com/patched"
# annotation_path == "/metadata/annotations/example.com~1patched"

patch = JsonPatch().add(annotation_path, "true")

# Or from raw tokens
label_path = JsonPointer.from_tokens("metadata", "labels", "version")
patch = patch.replace(label_path, "v2")

JSON Pointer escaping

Per RFC 6901, / inside a key is escaped as ~1 and ~ is escaped as ~0. For example, the annotation key example.com/patched becomes the path segment example.com~1patched.

Kubex can do this for you — pass a JsonPointer instead of a raw string: JsonPointer.from_tokens("metadata", "annotations", "example.com/patched") or JsonPointer("/metadata") / "annotations" / "example.com/patched". Both yield /metadata/annotations/example.com~1patched with the slash escaped automatically.

You can also construct a JsonPatch from a list of operation objects directly:

from kubex.core.patch import JsonPatch
from kubex.core.json_patch import JsonPatchAdd, JsonPatchRemove

patch = JsonPatch(
    [
        JsonPatchAdd(path="/metadata/labels/env", value="staging"),
        JsonPatchRemove(path="/metadata/labels/old-env"),
    ]
)

docs.title: ApplyPatch (server-side apply)
docs.text:
Server-side apply sends the fields you want to own; the API server merges them into the live object and records field_manager as their owner. It creates the object if it does not exist yet. A field_manager is required, and force=True takes over fields currently owned by another manager instead of failing with 409 Conflict:

from kubex.core.patch import ApplyPatch

patched = await api.patch(
    "example-deploy",
    ApplyPatch(
        Deployment(
            metadata=ObjectMetadata(name="example-deploy"),
            spec=DeploymentSpec(
                replicas=2,
                selector=LabelSelector(match_labels={"app": "example"}),
                template=PodTemplateSpec(
                    metadata=ObjectMetadata(labels={"app": "example"}),
                    spec=PodSpec(
                        containers=[Container(name="nginx", image="nginx:latest")]
                    ),
                ),
            ),
        )
    ),
    field_manager="my-controller",
    force=True,
)

Only the fields you set on the model are sent (exclude_unset), plus apiVersion and kind, which are always included — taken from the target resource, so you never need to set them yourself. The body is serialized as JSON (valid YAML, and what kubectl apply --server-side sends), so timestamps such as a condition's lastTransitionTime use their RFC 3339 wire format. metadata.managedFields is always stripped (the server rejects it in an apply body), so an object returned by get() can be modified and applied back directly.

docs.title: Patch options
docs.text:
All patch types accept these optional keyword arguments on api.patch():

Parameter Description dry_run Validate without persisting (True, "All" or DryRun.ALL) field_manager Field manager name recorded in managedFields; required for ApplyPatch force Force apply even when field ownership conflicts (ApplyPatch only) field_validation "Strict", "Warn" (the server default) or "Ignore" — or the FieldValidation enum 
patched = await api.patch(
    "example-deploy",
    merge_patch,
    dry_run=True,
    field_manager="my-controller",
)

docs.title: Full example from examples/patch_deployment.py
docs.text:
from typing import cast

from kubex.api import Api
from kubex.client import create_client
from kubex.core.patch import ApplyPatch, JsonPatch, MergePatch, StrategicMergePatch
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.apps.v1.deployment import Deployment
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.apps.v1.deployment_spec import DeploymentSpec
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.container import Container
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.pod_spec import PodSpec
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.pod_template_spec import PodTemplateSpec
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.meta.v1.label_selector import LabelSelector
from kubex_core.models.metadata import ObjectMetadata


async def main() -> None:
    client = await create_client()
    async with client:
        api: Api[Deployment] = Api(Deployment, client=client, namespace="default")

        deployment = await api.create(
            Deployment(
                metadata=ObjectMetadata(
                    name="example-deploy", labels={"app": "example"}
                ),
                spec=DeploymentSpec(
                    replicas=1,
                    selector=LabelSelector(match_labels={"app": "example"}),
                    template=PodTemplateSpec(
                        metadata=ObjectMetadata(labels={"app": "example"}),
                        spec=PodSpec(
                            containers=[Container(name="nginx", image="nginx:latest")]
                        ),
                    ),
                ),
            ),
        )
        name = cast(str, deployment.metadata.name)

        try:
            # MergePatch — update replicas
            merge_patch = MergePatch(
                Deployment(
                    metadata=ObjectMetadata(),
                    spec=DeploymentSpec(
                        replicas=3,
                        selector=LabelSelector(match_labels={"app": "example"}),
                        template=PodTemplateSpec(
                            metadata=ObjectMetadata(labels={"app": "example"}),
                            spec=PodSpec(
                                containers=[
                                    Container(name="nginx", image="nginx:latest")
                                ]
                            ),
                        ),
                    )
                )
            )
            patched = await api.patch(name, merge_patch)
            print(
                f"After MergePatch: replicas={patched.spec and patched.spec.replicas}"
            )

            # StrategicMergePatch — add an annotation
            strategic_patch = StrategicMergePatch(
                Deployment(
                    metadata=ObjectMetadata(annotations={"example.com/patched": "true"})
                )
            )
            patched = await api.patch(name, strategic_patch)
            print(
                f"After StrategicMergePatch: annotations={patched.metadata.annotations}"
            )

            # JsonPatch — add a label
            json_patch = JsonPatch().add("/metadata/labels/version", "v1")
            patched = await api.patch(name, json_patch)
            print(f"After JsonPatch: labels={patched.metadata.labels}")

            # ApplyPatch — server-side apply: send the fields this manager owns.
            # apiVersion/kind are filled in automatically.
            apply_patch = ApplyPatch(
                Deployment(
                    metadata=ObjectMetadata(name=name),
                    spec=DeploymentSpec(
                        replicas=2,
                        selector=LabelSelector(match_labels={"app": "example"}),
                        template=PodTemplateSpec(
                            metadata=ObjectMetadata(labels={"app": "example"}),
                            spec=PodSpec(
                                containers=[
                                    Container(name="nginx", image="nginx:latest")
                                ],
                            ),
                        ),
                    ),
                )
            )
            patched = await api.patch(
                name, apply_patch, field_manager="kubex-example", force=True
            )
            print(
                f"After ApplyPatch: replicas={patched.spec and patched.spec.replicas}"
            )
        finally:
            await api.delete(name)

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
Kubex separates two independent timeout concepts:

  • HTTP client timeout (request_timeout) — how long to wait for the HTTP call to complete (connect + response).
  • Kubernetes server-side timeout (timeout_seconds) — sent as the timeoutSeconds query parameter; the API server closes the stream or returns a result after this many seconds. Spelled timeout_seconds consistently across list(), delete_collection(), watch(), and metadata.list().

docs.title: Timeout and TimeoutTypes
docs.text:
Timeout is the structured object for configuring HTTP-level timeouts:

from kubex.core.params import Timeout

t = Timeout(total=30.0)  # 30 s total
t = Timeout(connect=5.0, read=60.0)  # separate connect / read
t = Timeout(total=30.0, connect=5.0, read=25.0)  # granular override
Field Description total Overall wall-clock timeout in seconds for the whole request, on both backends. Also the default for unset granular fields. connect Timeout for establishing the TCP connection. read Timeout for reading the response body. write Timeout for writing the request body (httpx only). pool Timeout for acquiring a connection from the pool (httpx only).

TimeoutTypes = Timeout | float | int | None — wherever a timeout is accepted, you can pass a number (treated as total seconds), a Timeout object, or None to disable timeouts entirely.

docs.title: Setting a client-level default
docs.text:
Pass ClientOptions(timeout=…) to create_client() to apply a default to every request made by that client:

from kubex.client import ClientOptions, create_client
from kubex.core.params import Timeout

client = await create_client(
    options=ClientOptions(timeout=Timeout(total=30.0)),
)

If no options is provided (or timeout=..., the default), the underlying HTTP library's own default applies (httpx: 5 s per phase — connect, read, write, pool — with no overall cap; aiohttp: 300 s total, 30 s sock_connect).

A client-level default applies in full to regular (non-streaming) requests. Streaming calls only inherit its connection-setup part — see Watch and long-lived streams.

docs.title: Per-call override with request_timeout
docs.text:
Every Api method accepts request_timeout= to override the client default for that call alone. The parameter accepts TimeoutTypes:

# Use the client default (Ellipsis = "inherit from client")
pod = await api.get("my-pod")

# Override to 5 seconds for this call
pod = await api.get("my-pod", request_timeout=5)

# Fine-grained override
pod = await api.get("my-pod", request_timeout=Timeout(connect=2.0, read=10.0))

# Disable timeouts for this call (long-running operation)
big_list = await api.list(request_timeout=None)

docs.title: The Ellipsis sentinel
docs.text:
Value Meaning ... (Ellipsis, the default) Use the client-level timeout (or the HTTP library default if none was configured) None Disable timeouts for this call 5 / 5.0 5 seconds total for this call Timeout(...) Structured per-field timeout for this call

Passing request_timeout=... explicitly is the same as omitting it — both mean "use the client default."

docs.title: Watch and long-lived streams
docs.text:
Server-side default closes the stream

The Kubernetes API server applies its own default timeoutSeconds (usually somewhere between 30 and 60 minutes) when the client does not provide one. A watch() call will not stream forever — your loop must reconnect when the server closes the stream. Pass an explicit timeout_seconds= to make the bound visible in code, and combine with the resume-after-Gone pattern to keep the watch alive across reconnects.

A watch or a followed log stream legitimately goes quiet for long periods, so when request_timeout is not passed, api.watch(), api.metadata.watch() and api.logs.stream() use a connect-only timeout: the connection-setup bounds of the client default are kept (connect/pool, or total while connecting — the library defaults if ClientOptions.timeout is not set), and the read and total bounds are dropped. A stream therefore never fails just because no event arrived for a while.

An explicit request_timeout is applied to the stream as given — a short value will terminate the stream. (On streams, httpx applies a total per phase — e.g. as the longest allowed gap between chunks — rather than as a wall-clock limit; aiohttp applies it to the whole stream.)

# Connect-only (the default): runs until the server closes the stream
async for event in api.watch(timeout_seconds=300):
    ...

# No HTTP timeout at all, not even for connecting
async for event in api.watch(request_timeout=None, timeout_seconds=300):
    ...

Detecting a dead connection

Without a read timeout, a connection that dies silently (e.g. a dropped NAT entry, no TCP reset) keeps the stream waiting. To bound that, pass timeout_seconds and a slightly larger client-side request_timeout: the server ends a healthy stream after timeout_seconds, so hitting the client timeout means the connection is gone.

async for event in api.watch(timeout_seconds=300, request_timeout=330):
    ...

For log follows (which have no server-side timeout), use a generous read timeout instead, e.g. request_timeout=Timeout(connect=10, read=600).

Two timeout parameters on watch()

watch(timeout_seconds=N) tells the API server to close the stream after N seconds. watch(request_timeout=M) tells the HTTP client to abort the connection after M seconds. They are independent — set both if you want server-side control and a client-side safety net.

docs.title: When a timeout fires
docs.text:
A client-side timeout raises KubexTimeoutError on both backends — for regular requests, streams (including mid-stream) and WebSocket handshakes. It subclasses both KubexClientException and the built-in TimeoutError, so either except clause catches it:

from kubex.core.exceptions import KubexTimeoutError

try:
    pod = await api.get("my-pod", request_timeout=5)
except KubexTimeoutError:
    ...

Cancelling the calling task (e.g. an enclosing anyio.move_on_after()) is never converted: it propagates as the runtime's own cancellation.

docs.title: timeout_seconds on list() and delete_collection()
docs.text:
The timeout_seconds parameter on list() and delete_collection() is the Kubernetes server-side timeoutSeconds parameter, not the HTTP client timeout. It limits how long the API server will process the request:

# Server-side: abort the list after 10 s (Kubernetes timeoutSeconds)
pods = await api.list(timeout_seconds=10)

# Client-side: abort the HTTP call after 15 s (HTTP read timeout)
pods = await api.list(request_timeout=15)

docs.title: Watch
docs.text: api.watch() opens a long-lived HTTP stream and yields WatchEvent objects as the Kubernetes API server emits them. It is an async generator — use it inside an async for loop.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
from kubex.api import Api
from kubex.client import create_client
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.pod import Pod

client = await create_client()
async with client:
    api: Api[Pod] = Api(Pod, client=client, namespace="default")
    async for event in api.watch():
        print(event.type, event.object.metadata.name)

docs.title: WatchEvent
docs.text:
Each yielded value is a WatchEvent[ResourceType]:

Attribute Type Description event.type EventType ADDED, MODIFIED, DELETED, or BOOKMARK event.object ResourceType | Bookmark Fully parsed resource (or Bookmark for bookmark events)

ERROR events are never yielded: the generator raises the matching exception instead — most importantly Gone (HTTP 410) when the requested resourceVersion is too old. See Resuming after Gone.

from kubex.core.watch_event import EventType

async for event in api.watch():
    match event.type:
        case EventType.ADDED:
            print(f"new pod: {event.object.metadata.name}")
        case EventType.DELETED:
            print(f"pod gone: {event.object.metadata.name}")

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Pass label_selector= or field_selector= to narrow the stream:

async for event in api.watch(label_selector="app=nginx"):
    ...

docs.title: Bookmarks and allow_bookmarks
docs.text:
Pass allow_bookmarks=True to request periodic BOOKMARK events from the server. Bookmark events carry an up-to-date resourceVersion in event.object.metadata.resource_version but no other data — they are checkpoints, not data.

The main reason to enable bookmarks is to keep an up-to-date resourceVersion even when the watched resources rarely change. Without bookmarks the saved resourceVersion ages with every quiet minute, and is far more likely to have been compacted (HTTP 410 Gone) by the time you reconnect.

async for event in api.watch(allow_bookmarks=True, namespace=None):
    if event.type == EventType.BOOKMARK:
        rv = event.object.metadata.resource_version
        print(f"checkpoint: resourceVersion={rv}")

docs.title: Watching across all namespaces
docs.text:
Pass namespace=None to watch across every namespace, even when the Api was created with a default namespace:

async for event in api.watch(namespace=None):
    ns = event.object.metadata.namespace
    name = event.object.metadata.name
    print(f"{event.type}: {ns}/{name}")

docs.title: send_initial_events pattern
docs.text:
send_initial_events=True makes the stream start with synthetic ADDED events for every existing resource, then a BOOKMARK annotated with k8s.io/initial-events-end: "true", then live updates — current state and future changes in one stream. The server requires bookmarks for this, so allow_bookmarks defaults to True when send_initial_events=True (passing allow_bookmarks=False together with it raises ValueError). It needs the API server's WatchList feature; a server without it rejects the request with 422.

async for event in api.watch(send_initial_events=True):
    if event.type == EventType.BOOKMARK:
        annotations = event.object.metadata.annotations or {}
        if annotations.get("k8s.io/initial-events-end") == "true":
            print("initial state complete, watching for changes now")
        continue
    print(event.type, event.object.metadata.name)

Not every bookmark marks the end of the initial events — periodic checkpoint bookmarks look the same apart from the annotation.

docs.title: Resuming after Gone
docs.text:
A watch does not last forever. The server ends the stream cleanly after timeout_seconds (or its own default, usually 30–60 minutes), and it raises Gone (HTTP 410) — on connect, or as an ERROR event mid-stream — when the resourceVersion you resume from has been compacted away. A long-running watcher therefore tracks the last resourceVersion it saw, resumes from it after a normal end of stream, and re-lists to get a fresh one after Gone. Bookmarks keep that resourceVersion current while nothing changes, which makes Gone far less likely:

from kubex.core.exceptions import Gone
from kubex.core.watch_event import EventType


async def watch_forever(api: Api[Pod]) -> None:
    resource_version: str | None = None
    while True:
        if resource_version is None:
            # (Re-)list: the current state plus a resourceVersion to watch from.
            pods = await api.list()
            for pod in pods.items:
                handle_existing(pod)
            resource_version = pods.metadata.resource_version
        try:
            async for event in api.watch(
                resource_version=resource_version, allow_bookmarks=True
            ):
                resource_version = (
                    event.object.metadata.resource_version or resource_version
                )
                if event.type != EventType.BOOKMARK:
                    handle(event)
        except Gone:
            # Too old to resume from: start over with a fresh list.
            resource_version = None
        # A normal end of stream (server-side timeout) resumes from
        # resource_version on the next iteration.

Events between the list and the watch are not lost: watching from the list's resourceVersion delivers everything that changed after it. Changes that happened while the watcher was disconnected for longer than the server keeps history are covered by the re-list, so handle_existing should reconcile (update or create local state, and drop objects that no longer exist) rather than assume a clean slate.

docs.title: Server-side timeout
docs.text:
Pass timeout_seconds= to set a server-side timeout on the watch call (sent as the Kubernetes timeoutSeconds query parameter). The server closes the stream cleanly after this many seconds and the async for loop simply ends; reconnect as shown above:

async for event in api.watch(timeout_seconds=60):
    ...

docs.title: Client-side timeouts
docs.text: A watch can stay quiet for minutes, so it does not inherit the client's short request timeouts: when request_timeout is left unset, a watch stream only applies the connect timeout and otherwise waits for the server to send events or end the stream (bound it with timeout_seconds instead). Passing an explicit request_timeout applies it as given — a short read or total timeout will cut off a quiet stream with a timeout error, so only do that deliberately (or pass request_timeout=None to disable client-side timeouts entirely).

docs.title: Example from examples/watch_pods.py
docs.text:
asyncio-only example

This example uses asyncio.create_task and asyncio.CancelledError, which are asyncio-specific. Trio users should replace these with anyio.create_task_group() instead.

import asyncio
from contextlib import suppress
from typing import cast

from kubex.api import Api
from kubex.client import create_client
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.container import Container
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.pod import Pod
from kubex.k8s.v1_35.core.v1.pod_spec import PodSpec
from kubex_core.models.metadata import ObjectMetadata


async def watcher(pod_api: Api[Pod]) -> None:
    async for event in pod_api.watch(allow_bookmarks=True, namespace=None):
        print(event)


async def main() -> None:
    client = await create_client()
    async with client:
        api: Api[Pod] = Api(Pod, client=client, namespace="default")
        _watcher = asyncio.create_task(watcher(api))
        pod_name: str | None = None
        try:
            _pod = await api.create(
                Pod(
                    metadata=ObjectMetadata(generate_name="example-pod-"),
                    spec=PodSpec(containers=[Container(name="example", image="nginx")]),
                ),
            )
            pod_name = cast(str, _pod.metadata.name)
        finally:
            if pod_name is not None:
                print(await api.delete(pod_name))
            _watcher.cancel()
            with suppress(asyncio.CancelledError):
                await _watcher

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:

Bases: Generic[ResourceType]

API for interacting with a Kubernetes resource type.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default resource_type Type[ResourceType]

The resource model class to operate on, e.g. Pod.

required client BaseClient

The client used to send requests.

required namespace ApiNamespaceTypes

The default namespace for this API's calls; each method can override it. If omitted, a namespace-scoped resource uses the client's configured namespace (the kubeconfig context's namespace, or the pod's own namespace in-cluster). Pass None for no default, which means "all namespaces" for list, watch and delete_collection. Cluster-scoped resources never get a namespace; passing one for them raises ValueError.

Ellipsis

namespace is given for a cluster-scoped resource.

def __init__(
    self,
    resource_type: Type[ResourceType],
    client: BaseClient,
    *,
    namespace: ApiNamespaceTypes = Ellipsis,
) -> None:
    self._resource = resource_type
    self._client = client
    self._request_builder = RequestBuilder(
        resource_config=resource_type.__RESOURCE_CONFIG__,
    )
    scope = self._resource.__RESOURCE_CONFIG__.scope
    if namespace is Ellipsis:
        # Unspecified: seed from the client's configured namespace, but only
        # for namespace-scoped resources -- a cluster-scoped resource must
        # never receive a namespace, configured or not. An explicit `None`
        # (rather than omitting the argument) still means "all namespaces"
        # and is never overridden by the client's configured namespace.
        # An empty configured namespace (e.g. `namespace: ""` in a kubeconfig
        # context) means "not set", not an empty path segment.
        namespace = (
            client.configuration.namespace or None
            if scope == Scope.NAMESPACE
            else None
        )
    self._namespace = namespace
    ensure_optional_namespace(namespace, self._namespace, scope)
    self.metadata = MetadataAccessor(
        client=self._client,
        request_builder=self._request_builder,
        namespace=self._namespace,
        scope=self._resource.__RESOURCE_CONFIG__.scope,
        resource_type=self._resource,
    )

async def create(
    self,
    data: ResourceType,
    *,
    namespace: ApiNamespaceTypes = Ellipsis,
    dry_run: DryRunTypes = None,
    field_manager: str | None = None,
    request_timeout: ApiRequestTimeoutTypes = Ellipsis,
) -> ResourceType:
    """Create a resource.

    Args:
        data: The resource instance to create.
        namespace: The namespace to create the resource in. If not provided,
            the namespace provided when creating the API will be used.
            The namespace is required for namespaced resources.
            If namespace is provided for cluster-scoped resources, an error will be raised.
        dry_run: Validate the request without persisting anything (``True``,
            ``"All"`` or ``DryRun.ALL``).
        field_manager: The field manager name recorded in ``managedFields`` as
            the owner of the fields this request sets.
        request_timeout: HTTP-level timeout override for this call. A number is
            interpreted as the total timeout in seconds. Pass ``None`` to disable
            timeouts entirely for this call. Omit to use the client default.

    Returns:
        ResourceType: the created resource instance, as stored by the API server.

    Raises:
        ValueError: an argument is invalid, e.g. a namespace that is missing for
            a namespace-scoped resource or given for a cluster-scoped one, or an
            unknown option value (e.g. for ``dry_run``).
        Conflict: a resource with this name already exists.
        KubexApiError: the API server rejected the request; the subclass
            matches the HTTP status (e.g. ``Forbidden``, ``UnprocessableEntity``).
        KubexConnectionError: the API server could not be reached.
        KubexTimeoutError: the request timed out on the client side.
        ConfigurationError: credentials could not be obtained, e.g. an exec
            plugin or OIDC token refresh failed.
    """
    _namespace = ensure_required_namespace(
        namespace, self._namespace, self._resource.__RESOURCE_CONFIG__.scope
    )
    options = PostOptions(dry_run=dry_run, field_manager=field_manager)
    request = self._request_builder.create(
        _namespace,
        options,
        data.model_dump_json(by_alias=True, exclude_none=True),
        request_timeout=request_timeout,
    )
    response = await self._client.request(request)
    return self._resource.model_validate_json(response.content)

    namespace: ApiNamespaceTypes = Ellipsis,

    propagation_policy: PropagationPolicyTypes = None,
    preconditions: Precondition | None = None,
    request_timeout: ApiRequestTimeoutTypes = Ellipsis,

    """Delete the specified resource.

    Args:
        name: The name of the resource to delete.
        namespace: The namespace of the namespaced resource to delete. If not provided,
            the namespace provided when creating the API will be used.
            The namespace is required for namespaced resources.
            If namespace is provided for cluster-scoped resources, an error will be raised.
        dry_run: Validate the request without deleting anything (``True``,
            ``"All"`` or ``DryRun.ALL``).
        grace_period_seconds: The duration in seconds before the object should be
            deleted, overriding its default grace period. ``0`` deletes immediately.
        propagation_policy: Whether and how dependents are garbage collected:
            ``"Foreground"``, ``"Background"`` or ``"Orphan"`` (or the
            ``PropagationPolicy`` enum).
        preconditions: Conditions the object must meet to be deleted
            (``Precondition(uid=..., resource_version=...)``); the server returns

        request_timeout: HTTP-level timeout override for this call. A number is
            interpreted as the total timeout in seconds. Pass ``None`` to disable
            timeouts entirely for this call. Omit to use the client default.

            it has finalizers or a termination grace period); the returned

            [Resource deletion documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#resource-deletion).

            ``dry_run``).

        Conflict: ``preconditions`` do not hold.
        KubexApiError: the API server rejected the request; the subclass
            matches the HTTP status (e.g. ``Forbidden``, ``UnprocessableEntity``).
        KubexConnectionError: the API server could not be reached.
        KubexTimeoutError: the request timed out on the client side.
        ConfigurationError: credentials could not be obtained, e.g. an exec
            plugin or OIDC token refresh failed.
    """

        namespace, self._namespace, self._resource.__RESOURCE_CONFIG__.scope
    )

        dry_run=dry_run,
        grace_period_seconds=grace_period_seconds,
        propagation_policy=propagation_policy,
        preconditions=preconditions,
    )
    request = self._request_builder.delete(
        name, _namespace, options, request_timeout=request_timeout
    )
    response = await self._client.request(request)

        return Status.model_validate_json(response.content)

    send_initial_events: bool | None = None,
    resource_version: ResourceVersionTypes = None,
    timeout_seconds: int | None = None,
    request_timeout: ApiRequestTimeoutTypes = Ellipsis,
) -> AsyncGenerator[WatchEvent[ResourceType], None]:
    """Watch for changes to the specified resource.

    Args:
        namespace: The namespace to watch. If not provided,
            the namespace provided when creating the API will be used.
            Pass ``None`` to watch all namespaces.
            If namespace is provided for cluster-scoped resources, an error will be raised.
        label_selector: Only watch resources whose labels match this selector.
            For details look at [Label Selectors documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#label-selectors).
        field_selector: Only watch resources whose fields match this selector.
            For details look at [Field Selectors documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/).
        allow_bookmarks: Request periodic ``BOOKMARK`` events carrying a fresh
            ``resourceVersion``. Defaults to ``True`` when ``send_initial_events``
            is ``True`` (the server requires it); passing ``False`` together with
            ``send_initial_events=True`` raises ``ValueError``.
        send_initial_events: Start the stream with synthetic ``ADDED`` events for
            the current state, followed by a bookmark annotated with
            ``k8s.io/initial-events-end``.
        resource_version: Only deliver changes made after this resource version,
            e.g. the list ``metadata.resource_version`` from a previous
            ``list()``. If not provided, the stream starts with synthetic
            ``ADDED`` events for every existing resource and then follows
            changes. For details look at
            [Resource Version Semantics documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#semantics-for-watch).

            stream cleanly after it.
        request_timeout: HTTP-level timeout override for this call. A number is
            interpreted as the total timeout in seconds. Pass ``None`` to disable
            timeouts entirely for this call. Omit to use the client's default
            for streams, which does not cut off an idle watch. An explicit
            short read/total timeout will terminate a quiet stream.

    Yields:
        WatchEvent[ResourceType]: one event per change, with its ``type``
            (``ADDED``, ``MODIFIED``, ``DELETED`` or ``BOOKMARK``) and
            ``object`` (the resource, or a ``Bookmark`` for ``BOOKMARK``
            events). ``ERROR`` events are raised as exceptions instead.

    Raises:
        ValueError: an argument is invalid, e.g. a namespace given for a
            cluster-scoped resource, or ``allow_bookmarks=False`` together with
            ``send_initial_events=True``.
        Gone: the requested ``resource_version`` is too old (HTTP 410), either
            on connect or as an ``ERROR`` event mid-stream; re-list and watch
            again from the new ``resourceVersion``.
        KubexApiError: the API server rejected the request; the subclass
            matches the HTTP status (e.g. ``Forbidden``, ``UnprocessableEntity``).
        KubexConnectionError: the API server could not be reached, or the

        namespace, self._namespace, self._resource.__RESOURCE_CONFIG__.scope
    )

        label_selector=label_selector,
        field_selector=field_selector,
        allow_bookmarks=allow_bookmarks,
        send_initial_events=send_initial_events,
        resource_version=resource_version,
        timeout_seconds=timeout_seconds,
    )

        _namespace,
        options,
        request_timeout=request_timeout,
    )

        yield WatchEvent(self._resource, json.loads(line))

async def create_api(
    resource_type: Type[ResourceType],
    *,
    client: BaseClient | None = None,
    namespace: ApiNamespaceTypes = Ellipsis,
) -> Api[ResourceType]:
    """Create an API for the specified resource type.

    Args:
        resource_type: The resource type to create an API for.
        client: The client to use for the API. If not provided,
            a new client will be created.
        namespace: The namespace to use for the API. If set all
            operations will be performed in this namespace.
            The Api namespace can be overridden by passing a
            namespace to the individual methods. If omitted, a
            namespace-scoped resource falls back to the client's
            configured namespace (e.g. the in-cluster pod's own
            namespace); pass ``None`` explicitly for "all namespaces"
            instead. Cluster-scoped resources never receive a namespace.

    Returns:
        An Api instance for the specified resource type.

    Raises:
        ValueError: ``namespace`` is given for a cluster-scoped resource.
        ConfigurationError: no ``client`` was given and no configuration could be
            loaded (no usable kubeconfig, and not running inside a cluster).
        ImportError: no ``client`` was given and neither ``aiohttp`` nor ``httpx``
            is installed.
    """
    client = client or await create_client()
    return Api(resource_type, client=client, namespace=namespace)

Run a command and collect stdout/stderr until the channel closes.

.. warning::

Experimental. This WebSocket-based API is still under active development and may change in future releases without notice.

Unlike :meth:stream, the request_timeout bound (when provided) applies to both the handshake (via the per-call HTTP timeout propagated to the WebSocket upgrade) and the post-handshake command execution + status collection (via a separate wall-clock cancel scope that does not envelope teardown — see below). Ellipsis defers to the client default for the handshake without imposing an additional wall-clock bound; an explicit None disables timeouts entirely.

stdin is sent in frames of at most 32 KiB and then half-closed. A failure while sending it (e.g. the command exited without reading all of it) is logged, not raised: the result reflects what the server reported. Use :meth:ExecResult.raise_for_status to turn a non-successful status into an exception.

async def run(
    self,
    name: str,
    *,
    command: Sequence[str],
    container: str | None = None,
    namespace: ApiNamespaceTypes = Ellipsis,
    stdin: bytes | None = None,
    stdout: bool = True,
    stderr: bool = True,
    request_timeout: ApiRequestTimeoutTypes = Ellipsis,
) -> ExecResult:
    """Run a command and collect stdout/stderr until the channel closes.

    .. warning::

       **Experimental.** This WebSocket-based API is still under active
       development and may change in future releases without notice.

    Unlike :meth:`stream`, the ``request_timeout`` bound (when provided)
    applies to both the handshake (via the per-call HTTP timeout
    propagated to the WebSocket upgrade) and the post-handshake command
    execution + status collection (via a separate wall-clock cancel scope
    that does not envelope teardown — see below). The wall-clock bound is
    derived from ``Timeout.total`` if set, otherwise ``Timeout.read``
    (read's strict per-byte-inactivity semantics do not map cleanly onto
    a long-lived WebSocket session, so it is treated as a call-level
    upper bound here as a pragmatic approximation that prevents
    indefinite hangs). ``Ellipsis`` defers to the client default for the
    handshake without imposing an additional wall-clock bound; an
    explicit ``None`` disables timeouts entirely.

    ``stdin`` is sent in frames of at most 32 KiB and then half-closed. A
    failure while sending it (e.g. the command exited without reading
    all of it) is logged, not raised: the result reflects what the
    server reported. Use :meth:`ExecResult.raise_for_status` to turn a
    non-successful status into an exception.

    Args:
        name: The name of the Pod to run the command in.
        command: The command and its arguments, e.g. ``["cat", "/etc/hostname"]``.
            Must be a non-empty sequence of strings, not a single string.
        container: The container to run the command in. Required when the Pod
            has more than one container.
        namespace: The namespace of the Pod. If not provided,
            the namespace provided when creating the API will be used.
            The namespace is required for namespaced resources.
            If namespace is provided for cluster-scoped resources, an error will be raised.
        stdin: Bytes to send to the command's stdin, which is then closed.
            ``None`` (the default) does not open a stdin channel at all;
            ``b""`` opens it and closes it right away.
        stdout: Capture stdout.
        stderr: Capture stderr.
        request_timeout: Timeout override for this call, bounding both the
            handshake and the command's run; see above. A number is
            interpreted as the total timeout in seconds. Pass ``None`` to
            disable timeouts entirely. Omit to use the client default for the
            handshake only.

    Returns:
        ExecResult: the captured ``stdout`` and ``stderr`` bytes and the
            ``status`` the server reported (``None`` if it reported none).

    Raises:
        ValueError: an argument is invalid, e.g. an empty or malformed ``name``,
            or a namespace that is missing for a namespace-scoped resource or
            given for a cluster-scoped one; or ``command`` is empty.
        TypeError: ``command`` is a single string (or bytes) instead of a
            sequence of strings, or contains a non-string item.
        KubexApiError: the WebSocket handshake was rejected; the subclass matches
            the HTTP status (e.g. ``NotFound`` for a missing pod, ``BadRequest``
            for an unknown container, ``Forbidden``).
        KubexConnectionError: the API server could not be reached.
        KubexTimeoutError: the WebSocket handshake or the command did not finish
            within ``request_timeout``.
        KubexClientException: the WebSocket handshake failed for another reason,
            or the connection closed abnormally.
        ConfigurationError: credentials could not be obtained, or the httpx
            client is used without the ``httpx-ws`` extra installed.
    """
    # Resolve the wall-clock bound for the post-handshake portion.
    # ``Ellipsis`` and a ``Timeout`` whose ``total`` and ``read`` are
    # both unset leave ``delay`` as ``None`` — ``anyio.fail_after(None)``
    # is a no-op cancel scope, so the only bound on the call in those
    # cases is whatever the handshake timeout enforces (set via
    # ``request_timeout`` propagation below).
    delay: float | None = None
    if request_timeout is not Ellipsis:
        coerced: Timeout | None = Timeout.coerce(request_timeout)
        if coerced is not None:
            delay = coerced.total if coerced.total is not None else coerced.read

    # The handshake is bounded by ``request_timeout`` propagation into
    # the per-backend WebSocket upgrade (see ``HttpxClient`` /
    # ``AioHttpClient``). The wall-clock ``fail_after`` below covers
    # only the post-handshake portion — keeping it *inside* the
    # ``async with session`` block ensures ``StreamSession.__aexit__``
    # (and the underlying ``connection.close()``) runs in an
    # un-cancelled scope so the HTTP/WebSocket transport is always
    # released, even when the deadline fires mid-call.
    session = await self._open_session(
        name,
        command=command,
        container=container,
        namespace=namespace,
        stdin=stdin is not None,
        stdout=stdout,
        stderr=stderr,
        tty=False,
        request_timeout=request_timeout,
    )
    stdout_buf = bytearray()
    stderr_buf = bytearray()
    status: Status | None = None
    async with session:

        async def _drain(
            stream: MemoryObjectReceiveStream[bytes], buf: bytearray
        ) -> None:
            async for chunk in stream:
                buf.extend(chunk)

        async def _write_stdin(data: bytes) -> None:
            # Like client-go, a failed stdin copy does not decide the
            # outcome: the command may have exited without reading all
            # of its input, and the read side still reports its status.
            # A broken connection surfaces there as well.
            try:
                await session.stdin.write(data)
                await session.close_stdin()
            except Exception as exc:
                _logger.debug("exec stdin write failed: %r", exc)

        # ``anyio.fail_after`` raises a bare ``TimeoutError`` at scope
        # exit when the deadline fires. The exec layer normalises every
        # other WebSocket-level failure to ``KubexClientException``
        # (see ``_resolve_protocol`` and the per-backend handshake
        # handlers), so convert here too — callers that
        # ``except KubexClientException`` for exec errors must observe
        # a timed-out ``run()`` consistently.
        try:
            with anyio.fail_after(delay):
                async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
                    if stdin is not None:
                        tg.start_soon(_write_stdin, stdin)
                    # Both channels are drained concurrently: the read
                    # loop waits for a full channel, so draining only one
                    # could stall the session.
                    async with anyio.create_task_group() as readers:
                        readers.start_soon(_drain, session.stdout, stdout_buf)
                        readers.start_soon(_drain, session.stderr, stderr_buf)
                    status = await session.wait_for_status()
                    # The command has finished; unsent stdin is moot.
                    tg.cancel_scope.cancel()
        except TimeoutError as exc:
            raise KubexTimeoutError(
                f"exec call exceeded {delay}s wall-clock bound"
            ) from exc
        except BaseExceptionGroup as eg:
            # anyio 4 wraps exceptions raised by tasks in a task group
            # in a ``BaseExceptionGroup`` even when only a single task
            # failed. Unwrap a single-exception group so callers that
            # catch ``KubexClientException`` (the documented exec
            # exception type) observe failures directly instead of
            # having to reach into an exception group.
            if len(eg.exceptions) == 1:
                raise eg.exceptions[0] from None
            raise
    return ExecResult(
        stdout=bytes(stdout_buf), stderr=bytes(stderr_buf), status=status
    )

def raise_for_status(self) -> Self:
    """Raise :class:`ExecError` unless the command reported ``Success``.

    Covers non-zero exits as well as failures without an exit code (e.g.
    the binary does not exist) and a missing status. Returns ``self`` so
    it can be chained: ``(await api.exec.run(...)).raise_for_status()``.

    Returns:
        Self: this result, unchanged, when the status is ``Success``.

    Raises:
        ExecError: the status is missing or is not ``Success``. Its message is
            the server's ``Status.message`` (or ``reason``) when there is one.
    """
    status = self.status
    if status is not None and status.status == "Success":
        return self
    if status is None:
        message = "exec finished without reporting a status"
    else:
        message = status.message or status.reason or "exec failed"
    raise ExecError(message, self)

PortForwardStream(
    session: PortForwardSession,
    port: int,
    data_channel_id: int,
    recv_stream: MemoryObjectReceiveStream[bytes],

Bases: ByteStream

Per-port bidirectional byte stream for the Kubernetes portforward subresource.

Wraps a PortForwardSession's data channel for a single port and implements anyio.abc.ByteStream so it integrates naturally with anyio byte-stream consumers.

Outbound send() encodes the payload as a channel frame addressed to the port's data channel. Inbound receive() reads from the session's per-port memory stream, buffering excess bytes to satisfy max_bytes slicing.

aclose() half-closes the data channel (idempotent via the underlying session helper) and prevents further send() calls. send_eof() performs the same half-close without locking out receives. On the v4 portforward subprotocol — which the kubelet requires — half-close is a local-only state change; the kubelet ignores wire CHANNEL_CLOSE frames on v4 and tears down the channel only when the session WebSocket closes.

def __init__(
    self,
    session: PortForwardSession,
    port: int,
    data_channel_id: int,
    recv_stream: MemoryObjectReceiveStream[bytes],
) -> None:
    self._session = session
    self._port = port
    self._data_channel_id = data_channel_id
    self._recv_stream = recv_stream
    self._buffer = b""
    self._send_closed = False
    # Keeps the frames of one ``send()`` contiguous and orders them
    # against ``send_eof()`` / ``aclose()``.
    self._send_lock = anyio.Lock()

async def aclose(self) -> None:
    """Close both directions of the stream.

    The sending side is closed as by ``send_eof()``. On the receiving side,
    ``receive()`` raises ``anyio.EndOfStream`` once any bytes left over from a
    partly read frame are returned, and data that arrives for this port
    afterwards is discarded, so an unread port no longer stalls the others.
    The session and its other ports stay open.
    """
    async with self._send_lock:
        self._send_closed = True
    try:
        await self._session.close_port_data(self._port)
    finally:
        self._recv_stream.close()

async def receive(self, max_bytes: int = 65536) -> bytes:
    """Receive bytes from the remote port, waiting until some arrive.

    A frame larger than ``max_bytes`` is returned over several calls.

    Args:
        max_bytes: The maximum number of bytes to return.

    Returns:
        bytes: between 1 and ``max_bytes`` bytes received from the pod.

    Raises:
        ValueError: ``max_bytes`` is not positive.
        anyio.EndOfStream: no more data will arrive: the kubelet closed the
            port's data channel, the session ended, or this stream was closed
            with ``aclose()``.
    """
    if max_bytes <= 0:
        raise ValueError(f"max_bytes must be positive, got {max_bytes}")
    while not self._buffer:
        try:
            self._buffer = await self._recv_stream.receive()
        except (anyio.ClosedResourceError, anyio.EndOfStream):
            raise anyio.EndOfStream()
    data = self._buffer[:max_bytes]
    self._buffer = self._buffer[max_bytes:]
    return data

async def send(self, item: bytes) -> None:
    """Send ``item`` to the remote port, split into frames of at most 32 KiB.

    Args:
        item: The bytes to send.

    Raises:
        anyio.ClosedResourceError: ``send_eof()`` or ``aclose()`` was called.
        KubexClientException: the session has already ended.
    """
    # The closed-flag check happens under the same lock that
    # send_eof()/aclose() take, so no data frame can follow a half-close.
    async with self._send_lock:
        if self._send_closed:
            raise anyio.ClosedResourceError("stream send side is closed")
        await self._session._send_data(self._data_channel_id, item)

Open portforward streams to the given ports as an async context manager.

.. warning::

Experimental. This WebSocket-based API is still under active development and may change in future releases without notice.

This is the low-level entry point: a single WebSocket multiplexes all requested ports, and the caller drives I/O directly in Python via per-port anyio.abc.ByteStream objects. No sockets are bound on the host — bytes never leave the process. Use this when your own code speaks to the pod (custom protocols, embedded clients, tests).

For the kubectl-style mode where external processes connect through a real local TCP port, use :meth:listen instead (which is built on top of this method).

Inbound data is never dropped; since the ports share one WebSocket, a port that is not read stalls all ports once its queue fills. Read every forwarded port (or aclose() the ones you don't need).

    self,
    name: str,
    *,
    ports: Sequence[int],
    namespace: ApiNamespaceTypes = Ellipsis,
    request_timeout: ApiRequestTimeoutTypes = Ellipsis,

    .. warning::

       **Experimental.** This WebSocket-based API is still under active
       development and may change in future releases without notice.

    all requested ports, and the caller drives I/O directly in Python via
    per-port ``anyio.abc.ByteStream`` objects. No sockets are bound on the
    host — bytes never leave the process. Use this when your own code
    speaks to the pod (custom protocols, embedded clients, tests).

    a real local TCP port, use :meth:`listen` instead (which is built on
    top of this method).

    port that is not read stalls all ports once its queue fills. Read
    every forwarded port (or ``aclose()`` the ones you don't need).

        ports: The pod ports to forward: 1 to 127 unique ports in 1..65535.
            Each becomes a key of ``streams`` and ``errors``.
        namespace: The namespace of the pod. If not provided,
            the namespace provided when creating the API will be used.

            handshake. A number is interpreted as the total timeout in
            seconds. Pass ``None`` to disable timeouts entirely. Omit to use
            the client default. It does not bound the session itself.

    Yields:
        PortForwarder: the per-port byte streams (``pf.streams[port]``) and
            error iterators (``pf.errors[port]``). The session's WebSocket is
            closed when the ``async with`` block exits.

            or a namespace that is missing for a namespace-scoped resource or
            given for a cluster-scoped one; or ``ports`` is empty,
            has duplicates or more than 127 entries, or a port is outside
            1..65535.
        TypeError: a port is not an ``int``.
        KubexApiError: the WebSocket handshake was rejected; the subclass matches
            the HTTP status (e.g. ``NotFound`` for a missing pod, ``Forbidden``).
        KubexConnectionError: the API server could not be reached.
        KubexTimeoutError: the WebSocket handshake timed out.
        KubexClientException: the WebSocket handshake failed for another reason,
            or the connection closed abnormally.

            client is used without the ``httpx-ws`` extra installed.

        name,
        ports=ports,
        namespace=namespace,
        request_timeout=request_timeout,
    )

        yield PortForwarder(session)

Open local TCP listeners and forward bytes bidirectionally to remote ports.

.. warning::

Experimental. This WebSocket-based API is still under active development and may change in future releases without notice.

This is the high-level, kubectl-style entry point: real OS sockets are bound on local_host:local_port so that any process on the host (curl, psql, a browser, …) can connect to the pod through a local port. Each accepted local connection opens its own portforward WebSocket session bound to that single remote port — one session per connection, matching kubectl port-forward semantics. The method itself yields None; you don't drive I/O through it.

For the low-level mode where your own Python code reads/writes bytes directly without binding any sockets, use :meth:forward instead (which this method is built on top of).

When the remote side finishes (or the kubelet reports an error), the local connection is closed; a local half-close (EOF) keeps the connection open until the remote response is complete. The v4 protocol cannot pass that EOF to the pod, so after a local client disconnects its connection stays open until the pod closes it or sends more data. Failures on individual connections (including a rejected WebSocket handshake) are logged to the kubex.portforward logger rather than raised.

@asynccontextmanager
async def listen(
    self,
    name: str,
    *,
    port_map: Mapping[int, int],
    local_host: str = "127.0.0.1",
    namespace: ApiNamespaceTypes = Ellipsis,
    request_timeout: ApiRequestTimeoutTypes = Ellipsis,
) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    """Open local TCP listeners and forward bytes bidirectionally to remote ports.

    .. warning::

       **Experimental.** This WebSocket-based API is still under active
       development and may change in future releases without notice.

    This is the **high-level**, kubectl-style entry point: real OS sockets
    are bound on ``local_host:local_port`` so that any process on the host
    (``curl``, ``psql``, a browser, …) can connect to the pod through a
    local port. Each accepted local connection opens its own portforward
    WebSocket session bound to that single remote port — one session per
    connection, matching ``kubectl port-forward`` semantics. The method
    itself yields ``None``; you don't drive I/O through it.

    For the low-level mode where your own Python code reads/writes bytes
    directly without binding any sockets, use :meth:`forward` instead
    (which this method is built on top of).

    When the remote side finishes (or the kubelet reports an error), the
    local connection is closed; a local half-close (EOF) keeps the
    connection open until the remote response is complete. The v4
    protocol cannot pass that EOF to the pod, so after a local client
    disconnects its connection stays open until the pod closes it or
    sends more data. Failures on individual connections (including a
    rejected WebSocket handshake) are logged to the ``kubex.portforward``
    logger rather than raised.

    Args:
        name: The name of the pod.
        port_map: Maps each **remote port** (on the pod) to the **local port**
            to listen on. Example: ``{80: 18080}`` opens a local listener on
            port 18080 that forwards to the pod's port 80.
        local_host: The local address the listeners bind to. The default,
            ``127.0.0.1``, only accepts connections from this host.
        namespace: The namespace of the pod. If not provided,
            the namespace provided when creating the API will be used.
            The namespace is required for namespaced resources.
            If namespace is provided for cluster-scoped resources, an error will be raised.
        request_timeout: HTTP-level timeout override for the WebSocket
            handshake of each accepted connection. A number is interpreted as
            the total timeout in seconds. Pass ``None`` to disable timeouts
            entirely. Omit to use the client default. It does not bound the
            connections themselves.

    Yields:
        None: the listeners stay open while the ``async with`` block runs;
            leaving it closes them and tears down open connections.

    Raises:
        ValueError: ``port_map`` is empty, a port is outside 1..65535, or two
            remote ports map to the same local port.
        TypeError: a port is not an ``int``.
    """
    if not port_map:
        raise ValueError("port_map must contain at least one entry")
    # Validate ports up front so a config error fails at context entry
    # instead of being deferred to the first incoming connection where
    # it would surface as a swallowed log line. Booleans are rejected
    # explicitly because ``bool`` is an ``int`` subclass — without this,
    # ``port_map={80: False}`` would silently bind port 0 (ephemeral),
    # which the caller has no way to discover since ``listen()`` yields
    # ``None``.
    for remote_port, local_port in port_map.items():
        if isinstance(remote_port, bool) or not isinstance(remote_port, int):
            raise TypeError(
                f"remote port must be int, got {type(remote_port).__name__}"
            )
        if not 1 <= remote_port <= 65535:
            raise ValueError(f"remote port {remote_port} out of range 1..65535")
        if isinstance(local_port, bool) or not isinstance(local_port, int):
            raise TypeError(
                f"local port must be int, got {type(local_port).__name__}"
            )
        if not 1 <= local_port <= 65535:
            raise ValueError(f"local port {local_port} out of range 1..65535")
    local_ports = list(port_map.values())
    if len(set(local_ports)) != len(local_ports):
        raise ValueError(f"duplicate local ports in port_map: {local_ports}")
    async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
        for remote_port, local_port in port_map.items():
            await tg.start(
                self._serve_port,
                name,
                remote_port,
                local_port,
                local_host,
                namespace,
                request_timeout,
            )
        try:
            yield
        finally:
            tg.cancel_scope.cancel()

        KubexTimeoutError: the request timed out on the client side.
        ConfigurationError: credentials could not be obtained, e.g. an exec
            plugin or OIDC token refresh failed.
    """
    _namespace = ensure_required_namespace(namespace, self._namespace, self._scope)
    options = PatchOptions(
        dry_run=dry_run,
        field_manager=field_manager,
        force=force,
        field_validation=field_validation,
    )
    request = self._request_builder.patch_metadata(
        name, _namespace, options, patch, request_timeout=request_timeout
    )
    response = await self._client.request(request)
    return PartialObjectMetadata.model_validate_json(response.content)

    self,
    *,
    namespace: ApiNamespaceTypes = Ellipsis,
    label_selector: str | None = None,
    field_selector: str | None = None,
    allow_bookmarks: bool | None = None,
    send_initial_events: bool | None = None,
    resource_version: ResourceVersionTypes = None,
    timeout_seconds: int | None = None,
    request_timeout: ApiRequestTimeoutTypes = Ellipsis,
) -> AsyncGenerator[
    WatchEvent[PartialObjectMetadata],
    None,
]:
    """Watch for metadata changes of resources.

    Args:
        namespace: The namespace to watch. If not provided,
            the namespace provided when creating the API will be used.
            Pass ``None`` to watch all namespaces.
            If namespace is provided for cluster-scoped resources, an error will be raised.
        label_selector: Only watch resources whose labels match this selector.
            For details look at [Label Selectors documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#label-selectors).
        field_selector: Only watch resources whose fields match this selector.
            For details look at [Field Selectors documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/).
        allow_bookmarks: Request periodic ``BOOKMARK`` events carrying a fresh
            ``resourceVersion``. Defaults to ``True`` when ``send_initial_events``
            is ``True`` (the server requires it); passing ``False`` together with
            ``send_initial_events=True`` raises ``ValueError``.
        send_initial_events: Start the stream with synthetic ``ADDED`` events for
            the current state, followed by a bookmark annotated with
            ``k8s.io/initial-events-end``.
        resource_version: Only deliver changes made after this resource version,
            e.g. the list ``metadata.resource_version`` from a previous
            ``list()``. If not provided, the stream starts with synthetic
            ``ADDED`` events for every existing resource and then follows
            changes. For details look at
            [Resource Version Semantics documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#semantics-for-watch).
        timeout_seconds: Server-side timeout (in seconds); the server ends the
            stream cleanly after it.
        request_timeout: HTTP-level timeout override for this call. A number is
            interpreted as the total timeout in seconds. Pass ``None`` to disable
            timeouts entirely for this call. Omit to use the client's default
            for streams, which does not cut off an idle watch. An explicit
            short read/total timeout will terminate a quiet stream.

    Yields:
        WatchEvent[PartialObjectMetadata]: one event per change, with its ``type``
            (``ADDED``, ``MODIFIED``, ``DELETED`` or ``BOOKMARK``) and ``object``
            (the resource's metadata, or a ``Bookmark`` for ``BOOKMARK`` events).
            ``ERROR`` events are raised as exceptions instead.

    Raises:
        ValueError: an argument is invalid, e.g. a namespace given for a
            cluster-scoped resource, or ``allow_bookmarks=False`` together
            with ``send_initial_events=True``.
        Gone: the requested ``resource_version`` is too old (HTTP 410), either
            on connect or as an ``ERROR`` event mid-stream; re-list and watch
            again from the new ``resourceVersion``.
        KubexApiError: the API server rejected the request; the subclass
            matches the HTTP status (e.g. ``Forbidden``, ``UnprocessableEntity``).
        KubexConnectionError: the API server could not be reached, or the
            connection broke mid-stream.
        KubexTimeoutError: the request timed out on the client side, including
            mid-stream.
        ConfigurationError: credentials could not be obtained, e.g. an exec
            plugin or OIDC token refresh failed.
    """
    _namespace = ensure_optional_namespace(namespace, self._namespace, self._scope)
    options = WatchOptions(
        label_selector=label_selector,
        field_selector=field_selector,
        allow_bookmarks=allow_bookmarks,
        send_initial_events=send_initial_events,
        timeout_seconds=timeout_seconds,
        resource_version=resource_version,
    )
    request = self._request_builder.watch_metadata(
        _namespace,
        options,
        request_timeout=request_timeout,
    )
    async for line in self._client.stream_lines(request):
        yield WatchEvent(PartialObjectMetadata, json.loads(line))

StreamSession(
    connection: WebSocketConnection,
    protocol: ChannelProtocol,
    *,
    stdin: bool = False,
    stdout: bool = True,
    stderr: bool = True,
    tty: bool = False,
    buffer_size: float = _DEFAULT_CHANNEL_BUFFER,
